orient: Narrator: Lockwood, but the story jumps ahead to September 1802, about eight months after Chapter XXXI. He left for London in January and has not been back since. After the row of asterisks Nelly takes over once more and catches him up on what has happened at the Heights since he left, starting in the late winter of 1802.

notes.g: The year jumps to 1802: it is now September, eight months after Lockwood's last visit.

notes.t: devastate the moors of a friend
notes.g: Go shooting game birds on a friend's moorland estate.
notes.n: Lockwood's joke: a shooting party 'devastates' the grouse. The grouse season opens in August.

notes.g: The man who looks after travellers' horses at an inn.
A pub or inn beside the road.
Oats just cut, still green and unripe.
notes.n: A sign of a late harvest up in the cold hills.

notes.tr: That's from Gimmerton, look! They're always three weeks behind everyone else with their harvest.

notes.g: Now; here a word of emphasis, like 'look!'.

notes.t: Happen fourteen mile o’er th’ hills
notes.g: Maybe fourteen miles over the hills.
notes.n: 'Happen' means perhaps.

notes.g: At the Grange, which Lockwood is still renting.
notes.n: His one-year lease runs until October.

notes.g: A pub that also has rooms for travellers.
Coming back to the area (a joke).
Lockwood's manservant, who travels with him.
notes.n: A gentleman rarely travelled alone.

notes.t: moor-sheep cropping the short turf on the graves
notes.g: A hill sheep nibbling the grass on the graves.
notes.n: 'Turf' is grass with its matted roots. The churchyard lies right by the open moor.

notes.g: Steep, broad, rounded hills covered with heather.
The back part of the house, where the kitchen and servants are.
A pipe smoked slowly and thoughtfully.
notes.n: Old countrywomen often smoked clay pipes.

notes.tr: Mrs. Dean? No! She doesn't live here: she's up at the Heights.

notes.g: Yes, I keep the house: I'm the housekeeper.
Put me up in for the night.

notes.tr: The master! Why, who ever knew you were coming? You should have sent word. There's nothing either dry or fit to use about the place: nothing at all!
notes.n: 'Dry' matters: a bed left unused in a damp house could make a guest ill.
From an old word 'mense', meaning decency or good manners.
'Apparition' usually means a ghost, so Lockwood is joking about himself.

notes.g: A small brush for sweeping ashes from the fireplace.
An iron rod for stirring a fire.
Misused; used for the wrong purpose.
notes.n: A comic, made-up-sounding word, like Lockwood himself.

notes.g: Her trade; the tools of housekeeping.

notes.n: In other words, 'As far as I know.' 'Owt' means anything.

notes.g: At such a critical moment (Lockwood's joke about her flustered housework).
The private grounds around Thrushcross Grange.
A soft golden glow with no rays of sunlight.
It opened when I pushed it.
notes.n: On his first visits the gate was chained shut (Chapter I).

notes.m: 'Homely' meant simple and domestic, not ugly.

notes.g: Windows made of small panes held in a crisscross frame of lead.
An area where coal is mined, so fuel is cheap.
notes.n: That's why a fire burns even on a warm evening.

notes.g: The people living in the house.
notes.m: Residents of any house, not prisoners.

notes.g: Cathy sounding out a word for her pupil, stressing the part he got wrong.

notes.n: A change from the rough farmhand Lockwood met before.
'Spite' here means vexation at himself.

notes.g: Lockwood regrets not trying to win Cathy himself.
notes.n: Remember his daydream at the end of Chapter XXXI.

notes.t: the lowest pit in the infernal regions

notes.g: Mrs. Dean, Lockwood's housekeeper and the teller of the story.

notes.tr: I'd far rather have them swearing in my ears from morning till night than listen to you at all! It's a blazing shame that I can't open the blessed Bible without you striking up those songs in praise of Satan, and all the frightful wickedness that was ever born into the world! Oh, you're a real good-for-nothing, and she's another, and that poor lad will be lost between the two of you. Poor lad! He's bewitched, I'm certain of it. Oh Lord, judge them, for there's neither law nor justice among our rulers!
notes.n: 'She' is Cathy and 'the poor lad' is Hareton.

notes.g: Howsoever: in any way; at all.

notes.n: To strict Joseph, any secular song or ballad is the devil's music.
'Nowt' (nothing) can also mean a worthless person.

notes.t: norther law nor justice among wer rullers
notes.g: Neither law nor justice among our rulers.
notes.n: Joseph grumbles that the authorities no longer punish witchcraft. England's last witchcraft laws were repealed in 1736.
Witches and heretics were once burned at the stake on piles of fagots. Nelly is teasing Joseph.

notes.g: A traditional ballad that Nelly is singing.

notes.n: Dancing would shock Joseph even more.

notes.m: A time word, not 'in a straight line'.

notes.g: Moved here (like a plant dug up and replanted).
The former housekeeper at the Heights, whose account Nelly retold in Chapter XXX.
Leading me into the main living room.
notes.m: At the Heights 'the house' is the big family room (see Chapter I), not the whole building.

notes.g: I handle her business for her, as her agent.

notes.m: Since 'dinner' was at midday, the evening meal was 'supper'.

notes.n: A phrase from the King James Bible.

notes.g: Strong beer aged for a long time.
notes.n: Farmhouses brewed their own ale.

notes.tr: Wasn't it a crying scandal that she should have men calling on her at her age? And then to fetch them jugs of ale out of the master's cellar! He was truly ashamed to sit still and watch it.
notes.n: Lockwood reports Joseph's words, so Joseph's 'I' becomes 'he'.

notes.m: A 'follower' was a man courting a servant. Many employers banned them.
notes.n: Joseph pretends Lockwood is courting middle-aged Nelly.

notes.g: Stay still; bear to sit quietly.
A silver pint tankard brimming with foam.
notes.n: 'Ream' is a northern word for cream or froth.

notes.t: I was summoned to Wuthering Heights
notes.g: Nelly takes over the story again.
notes.n: She goes back to late January 1802, just after Lockwood left.

notes.g: Have the main living room to himself.
notes.m: 'The house' here is the family room, not the whole building.

notes.g: Making remarks meant for him to overhear.
A big, heavy horse for pulling farm carts.
One of the dogs at the Heights, the pointer from Chapter I.
Jobs done standing in one place.
Clockwork figures; machines that look like people.

notes.t: her wicked nonsense, as he would have called it
notes.g: Joseph would call any book but a religious one wicked.
His room: here, the main living room.
notes.m: 'Apartment' meant a room, not a flat.

notes.g: Stuck in the kitchen like a piece of furniture.

notes.n: Old guns sometimes split open when a barrel was damaged or overloaded.

notes.g: Of necessity; he had no choice.

notes.t: till he made it up again

notes.g: The day after Easter Sunday, a public holiday.
notes.n: In 1802 it fell in April. Fairs were often held on it.

notes.g: The village market, where cattle and goods were bought and sold.
Washing, starching and ironing the sheets and clothes.

notes.m: No sexual meaning: any short burst of speech.

notes.g: The stone slab in front of the fireplace.
You must acknowledge me (as your cousin).

notes.s: I shall have naught to do
notes.tr: I'll have nothing to do with you and your filthy pride and your damned mocking tricks! I'll go to hell, body and soul, before I look your way again. Get out of my way, now, this minute!

notes.n: Still common in northern England.
Nelly teases Joseph by borrowing his phrase later in the chapter.
In Yorkshire 'gate' can mean way or road, from Old Norse.
'Shoon' is an old plural of 'shoe'. He means: good enough even to clean her shoes.

notes.g: Female messenger or go-between (a playful word).
The person it was meant for.
Cathy, jokingly: she has hired Nelly as her messenger.

notes.t: the treaty had been ratified on both sides
notes.n: Nelly jokes as if two warring nations had signed a treaty.
Illustrated books were luxuries.

notes.t: his favourite’s endurance of her proximity
notes.g: Hareton putting up with her being so close.
notes.n: Joseph has always favoured Hareton.

notes.g: Paper money from the cattle he sold at the fair.

notes.t: the produce of the day’s transactions
notes.g: The money from the day's sales.

notes.s: Tak’ these in to t’ maister
notes.tr: Take these in to the master, lad, and stay there. I'll go up to my own room. This hole isn't decent or proper for the likes of us: we must get out and look for another.

notes.n: Joseph means the kitchen, spoiled for him by Cathy.

notes.g: Mantelpiece: the shelf above the fireplace.

notes.tr: Any books you leave, I'll take into the house, and it'll be a wonder if you ever find them again; so you can please yourself!
notes.n: 'The house' is the main living room, Heathcliff's territory.

notes.g: The house: the main living room.
It'll be a wonder; it'll be a lot.

notes.t: his library should pay for hers
notes.g: She would take his religious books in revenge.
Her secret visits to Linton at the Heights (Chapters XXIII–XXIV).
Turned into a gentleman just by wishing it.

notes.n: A 'philosopher' could mean someone who bears troubles calmly.

notes.t: The crown of all my wishes
notes.g: What I would like most of all.

notes.n: Nelly's own hope. Cathy is a widow and free to remarry.
